claim: In central nervous system (CNS) synapses, action potential-evoked neurotransmitter release is principally mediated by CaV2.1 calcium channels.
source: In central nervous system (CNS) synapses, action potential-evoked neurotransmitter release is principally mediated by CaV2.1 calcium channels (CaV2.1) and is highly dependent on the physical distance between CaV2.1 and synaptic vesicles (coupling).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the neuroscience field, supported by extensive prior research and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Action potential-evoked neurotransmitter release is highly dependent on the physical distance between CaV2.1 and synaptic vesicles (coupling).
source: In central nervous system (CNS) synapses, action potential-evoked neurotransmitter release is principally mediated by CaV2.1 calcium channels (CaV2.1) and is highly dependent on the physical distance between CaV2.1 and synaptic vesicles (coupling).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Neher and Sakaba, 2008 in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Various active zone proteins are proposed to control coupling and abundance of CaV2.1 through direct interactions with the CaV2.1 α1 subunit C-terminus at the active zone.
source: Although various active zone proteins are proposed to control coupling and abundance of CaV2.1 through direct interactions with the CaV2.1 α1 subunit C-terminus at the active zone, the role of these interaction partners is controversial.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations in the manuscript to prior literature proposing these interactions.

claim: The role of active zone protein interaction partners with CaV2.1 α1 subunit C-terminus is controversial.
source: Although various active zone proteins are proposed to control coupling and abundance of CaV2.1 through direct interactions with the CaV2.1 α1 subunit C-terminus at the active zone, the role of these interaction partners is controversial.
evidence: The manuscript cites disparate results from different model systems and knockout mouse models (Acuna et al., 2015; Atasoy et al., 2007; Butz et al., 1998; Cao et al., 2004; Das, 2016; Davydova et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2006; Hu et al., 2005; Kaeser et al., 2011; Wong et al., 2014; Wong and Stanley, 2010).

claim: A region in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit C-terminus between amino acids 2042 and 2061 directly controls fast synaptic vesicle release.
source: Our results identified a region that directly controlled fast synaptic vesicle release and vesicle docking at the active zone independent of CaV2.1 abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings showing dramatic reduction in 3 ms peak EPSC amplitude and slowdown in release kinetics with CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 mutants but not with Δ2061-2368 mutant (Figures 3, 4 and Tables 2, 3).

claim: A region in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit C-terminus between amino acids 2042 and 2061 controls vesicle docking at the active zone.
source: Our results identified a region that directly controlled fast synaptic vesicle release and vesicle docking at the active zone independent of CaV2.1 abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing specific reduction in docked vesicles (within 5 nm of membrane) in CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 mutants (Figure 5).

claim: The region between amino acids 2042 and 2061 in CaV2.1 α1 subunit controls fast vesicle release and docking independent of CaV2.1 abundance.
source: Our results identified a region that directly controlled fast synaptic vesicle release and vesicle docking at the active zone independent of CaV2.1 abundance.
evidence: This is supported by data showing no significant changes in Ca2+ current amplitudes with the mutants (Figure 2, Table 1) while showing dramatic effects on release and docking (Figures 3-5).

claim: Proposed individual direct interactions with active zone proteins are insufficient for CaV2.1 abundance.
source: In addition, proposed individual direct interactions with active zone proteins are insufficient for CaV2.1 abundance and coupling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in Ca2+ current amplitudes when binding sites for RIM1/2, MINT1, RBP, CASK, and secondary CaVβ4 were deleted (Figure 2, Table 1).

claim: Proposed individual direct interactions with active zone proteins are insufficient for CaV2.1 coupling.
source: In addition, proposed individual direct interactions with active zone proteins are insufficient for CaV2.1 abundance and coupling.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing no significant changes in release kinetics or RRP size when binding sites for RIM1/2, MINT1, RBP, CASK were deleted (CaV2.1Δ2365–2368, CaV2.1Δ2213–2368, CaV2.1Δ2061–2368) (Figure 3, Table 2).

claim: A critical determinant in regulating synaptic vesicle release probability and kinetics is coupling, the physical distance of SVs and voltage-gated calcium channels at the presynaptic terminal.
source: A critical determinant in regulating synaptic vesicle (SV) release probability and kinetics is coupling, the physical distance of SVs and voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) at the presynaptic terminal (Neher and Sakaba, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Neher and Sakaba, 2008.

claim: Differences in coupling distances between CaV2 VGCC subtypes underpin the differences in CaV2 VGCC subtype effectiveness in eliciting AP evoked release.
source: Differences in coupling distances between CaV2 VGCCs subtypes underpin the differences in CaV2 VGCC subtype effectiveness in eliciting AP evoked release and define the SV release mode in response to APs (Eggermann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eggermann et al., 2011.

claim: Nanodomain release mode involves a few tightly coupled VGCCs (<30 nm) triggering SV release.
source: They are: nanodomain, a few tightly coupled VGCCs (<30 nm), and microdomain, many loosely coupled VGCCs (~100 nm) trigger SV release (Baur et al., 2015; Eggermann et al., 2011; Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baur et al., 2015; Eggermann et al., 2011; Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005.

claim: Microdomain release mode involves many loosely coupled VGCCs (~100 nm) triggering SV release.
source: They are: nanodomain, a few tightly coupled VGCCs (<30 nm), and microdomain, many loosely coupled VGCCs (~100 nm) trigger SV release (Baur et al., 2015; Eggermann et al., 2011; Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baur et al., 2015; Eggermann et al., 2011; Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005.

claim: In the majority of central nervous system synapses, CaV2.1 VGCCs are the principal CaV subtype that supports AP mediated neurotransmitter release.
source: In the majority of central nervous system synapses, CaV2.1 VGCCs (CaV2.1) are the principal CaV subtype that supports AP mediated neurotransmitter release, and CaV2.1 channels are thought to exist in closest proximity to SVs compared to other CaV subtypes (Eggermann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eggermann et al., 2011 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: CaV2.1 channels are thought to exist in closest proximity to SVs compared to other CaV subtypes.
source: In the majority of central nervous system synapses, CaV2.1 VGCCs (CaV2.1) are the principal CaV subtype that supports AP mediated neurotransmitter release, and CaV2.1 channels are thought to exist in closest proximity to SVs compared to other CaV subtypes (Eggermann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eggermann et al., 2011.

claim: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit cytoplasmic C-terminus is mutated in a class of CaV2 channelopathies.
source: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit cytoplasmic C-terminus is mutated in a class of CaV2 channelopathies (Pietrobon, 2010) and contains many motifs implicated to directly interact with key active zone (AZ) proteins to control CaV2.1 coupling and abundance in the presynaptic terminal (Simms and Zamponi, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pietrobon, 2010.

claim: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit C-terminus contains many motifs implicated to directly interact with key active zone proteins to control CaV2.1 coupling and abundance in the presynaptic terminal.
source: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit cytoplasmic C-terminus is mutated in a class of CaV2 channelopathies (Pietrobon, 2010) and contains many motifs implicated to directly interact with key active zone (AZ) proteins to control CaV2.1 coupling and abundance in the presynaptic terminal (Simms and Zamponi, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Simms and Zamponi, 2014.

claim: The necessity and mechanism of action of C-terminal motifs in CaV2.1 α1 subunit are highly controversial due to disparate results from different model systems and knockout mouse models.
source: Nevertheless, the necessity and mechanism of action of these motifs are highly controversial due to disparate results from different model systems and from knockout mouse models of AZ proteins (Acuna et al., 2015; Atasoy et al., 2007; Butz et al., 1998; Cao et al., 2004; Das, 2016; Davydova et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2006; Hu et al., 2005; Kaeser et al., 2011; Wong et al., 2014; Wong and Stanley, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature showing disparate results.

claim: It is unclear whether the mechanisms that control coupling and abundance are interrelated or separable.
source: In addition, it is unclear whether the mechanisms that control coupling and abundance are interrelated or separable.
evidence: This represents a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The calyx of Held/MNTB synapse is a large glutamatergic axosomatic synapse.
source: To address these questions, we utilized the calyx of Held/Medial Nucleus of the Trapezoid Body (MNTB) synapse, a large glutamatergic axosomatic synapse, in which: (1) individual AZs ultrastructure and (2) CaV2 subtype abundance and proximity to SVs controlling SV release at the calyx of Held is similar to many other synapses (Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012).
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of the calyx of Held synapse, supported by citation to Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012.

claim: Individual AZ ultrastructure at the calyx of Held is similar to many other synapses.
source: To address these questions, we utilized the calyx of Held/Medial Nucleus of the Trapezoid Body (MNTB) synapse, a large glutamatergic axosomatic synapse, in which: (1) individual AZs ultrastructure and (2) CaV2 subtype abundance and proximity to SVs controlling SV release at the calyx of Held is similar to many other synapses (Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012.

claim: CaV2 subtype abundance and proximity to SVs controlling SV release at the calyx of Held is similar to many other synapses.
source: To address these questions, we utilized the calyx of Held/Medial Nucleus of the Trapezoid Body (MNTB) synapse, a large glutamatergic axosomatic synapse, in which: (1) individual AZs ultrastructure and (2) CaV2 subtype abundance and proximity to SVs controlling SV release at the calyx of Held is similar to many other synapses (Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012.

claim: Due to its experimental accessibility, molecular manipulations can be made exclusively in the presynaptic terminals of the calyx of Held.
source: Furthermore, due to its unparalleled experimental accessibility, molecular manipulations can be made exclusively in the presynaptic terminals (Wimmer et al., 2004; Young and Neher, 2009), and presynaptic Ca2+ currents can be recorded and correlated with synaptic vesicle release rates (Neher and Sakaba, 2001b), which allows for well-controlled measurements not achievable in other model systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wimmer et al., 2004; Young and Neher, 2009.

claim: Presynaptic Ca2+ currents can be recorded and correlated with synaptic vesicle release rates at the calyx of Held.
source: Furthermore, due to its unparalleled experimental accessibility, molecular manipulations can be made exclusively in the presynaptic terminals (Wimmer et al., 2004; Young and Neher, 2009), and presynaptic Ca2+ currents can be recorded and correlated with synaptic vesicle release rates (Neher and Sakaba, 2001b), which allows for well-controlled measurements not achievable in other model systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Neher and Sakaba, 2001b.

claim: The calyx of Held allows for well-controlled measurements not achievable in other model systems.
source: Furthermore, due to its unparalleled experimental accessibility, molecular manipulations can be made exclusively in the presynaptic terminals (Wimmer et al., 2004; Young and Neher, 2009), and presynaptic Ca2+ currents can be recorded and correlated with synaptic vesicle release rates (Neher and Sakaba, 2001b), which allows for well-controlled measurements not achievable in other model systems.
evidence: This is based on the unique experimental advantages of the calyx of Held system described in the citations.

claim: A novel intrinsic motif in the C-terminus regulates coupling.
source: Thus, we were able to identify a novel intrinsic motif in the C-terminus that regulates coupling and demonstrate that coupling and abundance are separable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that deletions in the 2042-2061 region affect coupling (release kinetics) without affecting Ca2+ current amplitudes (Figures 3-4, Tables 2-3).

claim: Coupling and abundance are separable mechanisms.
source: Thus, we were able to identify a novel intrinsic motif in the C-terminus that regulates coupling and demonstrate that coupling and abundance are separable.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that deletions affecting coupling (2042-2368, 2016-2368) do not affect Ca2+ current amplitudes (abundance), while deletions not affecting coupling (2365-2368, 2213-2368, 2061-2368) also do not affect abundance (Figures 2-4, Tables 1-2).

claim: The novel C-terminal region in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit regulates SV docking at the AZ.
source: Finally, we found that this novel C-terminal region in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit also regulates SV docking at the AZ.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing reduced docked vesicles in CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 mutants (Figure 5).

claim: Helper-Dependent Adenoviral vectors can package large amounts of foreign DNA.
source: HdAds can package large amounts of foreign DNA, which is critical as the CaV2.1 α1 subunit cDNA is larger than commonly used viral vectors (Lentz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lentz et al., 2012.

claim: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit cDNA is larger than commonly used viral vectors.
source: HdAds can package large amounts of foreign DNA, which is critical as the CaV2.1 α1 subunit cDNA is larger than commonly used viral vectors (Lentz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the size of the CaV2.1 α1 subunit cDNA, supported by citation.

claim: CaV2.1 full transcript is the longest CaV2.1 α1 subunit cDNA.
source: CaV2.1 full transcript (FT) is the longest CaV2.1 α1 subunit cDNA (Mus musculus NP_031604.3).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the CaV2.1 full transcript with reference to the NCBI accession number.

claim: CaV2.1 was successfully ablated at the calyx using HdAd Cre on a Cacna1a conditional knock-out background.
source: By testing Ca2+ current sensitivity to CaV2 subtype-specific blockers ω-Agatoxin IVA (Aga, CaV2.1-selective) and ω-Conotoxin GVIA (Cono, CaV2.2-selective), we confirmed that we could ablate CaV2.1 and subsequently rescue CaV2.1 abundance (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological data showing loss of ω-Agatoxin IVA-sensitive current in CKO condition (Figure 1E-F).

claim: CaV2.1 abundance was successfully rescued using HdAd CaV2.1 FT on a CaV2.1 null background.
source: By testing Ca2+ current sensitivity to CaV2 subtype-specific blockers ω-Agatoxin IVA (Aga, CaV2.1-selective) and ω-Conotoxin GVIA (Cono, CaV2.2-selective), we confirmed that we could ablate CaV2.1 and subsequently rescue CaV2.1 abundance (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological data showing restoration of ω-Agatoxin IVA-sensitive current in full transcript rescue condition (Figure 1E-F).

claim: CaV2.1Δ2365–2368 deletes the α1 subunit DDWC motif that is implicated to bind directly to RIM1/2 and MINT.
source: CaV2.1Δ2365–2368 deletes the α1 subunit DDWC motif that is implicated to bind directly to RIM1/2 and MINT (Kaeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the mutant construct with citation to Kaeser et al., 2011 for the binding interaction.

claim: CaV2.1Δ2213–2368 corresponds to a CaV2.1 α1 subunit splice variant which removes the RIM1/2, MINT1, RBP, and part of the CASK binding site and majority of PXXP motifs.
source: CaV2.1Δ2213–2368 corresponds to a CaV2.1 α1 subunit splice variant which removes the RIM1/2, MINT1, RBP, and part of the CASK binding site and majority of PXXP motifs (Soong et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a description of the mutant construct with citation to Soong et al., 2002 for the splice variant.

claim: CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 removes the complete CASK binding site, a proposed secondary CaVβ4 interaction site, and two remaining PXXP motifs in the α1 subunit.
source: CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 removes the complete CASK binding site, a proposed secondary CaVβ4 interaction site, and two remaining PXXP motifs in the α1 subunit (Figure 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the mutant construct with reference to figures showing the deletion regions.

claim: Expression of mutants lacking motifs located within the last 350 amino acids revealed no significant difference in Ca2+ current amplitudes compared to CaV2.1 FT rescue.
source: Analysis of the Ca2+ current as a function of voltage (I(V)) and tail currents revealed that expression of mutants lacking motifs located within the last 350 amino acids revealed no significant difference in Ca2+ current amplitudes or voltage dependent activation compared to CaV2.1 FT rescue (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing no statistically significant differences in maximal Ca2+ current amplitudes among mutants Δ2365–2368, Δ2213–2368, and Δ2016–2368 compared to FT rescue (Figure 2, Table 1).

claim: Expression of mutants lacking motifs located within the last 350 amino acids revealed no significant difference in voltage dependent activation compared to CaV2.1 FT rescue.
source: Analysis of the Ca2+ current as a function of voltage (I(V)) and tail currents revealed that expression of mutants lacking motifs located within the last 350 amino acids revealed no significant difference in Ca2+ current amplitudes or voltage dependent activation compared to CaV2.1 FT rescue (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing no statistically significant differences in voltage-dependent activation parameters (Vm, km, V0.5, k) among mutants compared to FT rescue (Table 1).

claim: The MINT1, RIM1/2, RBP, CASK proteins and the secondary CaVβ4 binding sites within the CaV2.1 α1 subunit C-terminus are not necessary for CaV2.1 localization to the presynaptic membrane.
source: Thus, the MINT1, RIM1/2, RBP, CASK proteins and the secondary CaVβ4 binding sites within the CaV2.1 α1 subunit C-terminus are not necessary for CaV2.1 localization to the presynaptic membrane.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing no significant reduction in Ca2+ current amplitudes when these binding sites were deleted (Figure 2, Table 1).

claim: CaV2.1Δ2061–2368 deletes up to the secondary CaVβ4 interaction in the α1 subunit.
source: CaV2.1Δ2061–2368 deletes up to the secondary CaVβ4 interaction in the α1 subunit and CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 deletes an additional arginine rich stretch in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit, not found in CaV2.2 and CaV2.3 and the final shared PXPP motif.
evidence: This is a description of the mutant construct.

claim: CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 deletes an additional arginine rich stretch in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit, not found in CaV2.2 and CaV2.3 and the final shared PXPP motif.
source: CaV2.1Δ2061–2368 deletes up to the secondary CaVβ4 interaction in the α1 subunit and CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 deletes an additional arginine rich stretch in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit, not found in CaV2.2 and CaV2.3 and the final shared PXPP motif.
evidence: This is a description of the mutant construct with information about sequence homology.

claim: A 3 ms step depolarization pulse selectively depletes SVs within ~50–80 nm of CaV2 VGCCs which participate in synchronous transmitter release (fast pool).
source: First we applied either a 3 ms step depolarization pulse (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) to the calyx which selectively depletes SVs within ~50–80 nm of CaV2 VGCCs (Chen et al., 2015) which participate in synchronous transmitter release (fast pool) (Chen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Lee et al., 2012.

claim: The fast pool is the relevant SV pool that supports AP-mediated release and is considered the readily-releasable pool (RRP).
source: The fast pool is the relevant SV pool that supports AP-mediated release and thus considered the readily-releasable pool (RRP) (Figures 3–4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 2) (Sakaba, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sakaba, 2006.

claim: A 30 ms step depolarization measures the entire pool of fusion competent SVs, all within ~200 nm of CaV2 and considered the total releasable pool.
source: Then we applied a 30 ms step depolarization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) which measures the entire pool of fusion competent SVs, all within ~200 nm of CaV2 and considered the total releasable pool (Chen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2012) (Figures 3–4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Lee et al., 2012.

claim: There were no differences in SV release between the CaV2.1 FT and wild-type calyces.
source: We found no differences in SV release between the CaV2.1 FT and wild-type calyces (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 2), indicating that exogenous expression of the CaV2.1 α1 subunit did not alter calyx/MNTB synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing wild-type and full transcript rescue conditions (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 2).

claim: Exogenous expression of the CaV2.1 α1 subunit did not alter calyx/MNTB synaptic transmission.
source: We found no differences in SV release between the CaV2.1 FT and wild-type calyces (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 2), indicating that exogenous expression of the CaV2.1 α1 subunit did not alter calyx/MNTB synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing no differences between wild-type and full transcript rescue.

claim: There was no change in presynaptic Ca2+ currents in response to 3 ms and 30 ms presynaptic depolarizations in all mutants.
source: In response to 3 ms and 30 ms presynaptic depolarizations, we found no difference in the presynaptic Ca2+ currents in all mutants, thus confirming our results depicted in Figure 2 (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in Ca2+ current amplitudes or charge among all mutants (Figure 3, Table 2).

claim: The 3 ms peak EPSC amplitude directly correlates to those SVs that are tightly coupled to CaV2 channels at the P9-11 calyx.
source: Since the 3 ms peak EPSC amplitude directly correlates to those SVs that are tightly coupled to CaV2 channels at the P9-11 calyx (Chen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2012), we measured the peak 3 ms EPSC peak amplitudes in all our deletion mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Lee et al., 2012.

claim: There was no change in 3 ms peak EPSC amplitudes with deletions from amino acid 2265 and beyond (CaV2.1Δ2365–2368, CaV2.1Δ2213–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2061–2368) compared to control.
source: Analysis of the 3 ms peak EPSC amplitudes revealed no change in the peak amplitudes with deletions from amino acid 2265 and beyond (CaV2.1Δ2365–2368, CaV2.1Δ2213–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2061–2368), when compared to control (CaV2.1 FT; Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no statistically significant differences in 3 ms EPSC amplitudes for these mutants (Figure 3, Table 2).

claim: There was a dramatic reduction in the 3 ms EPSC amplitudes with CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368.
source: However, we saw a dramatic reduction in the EPSC amplitudes with CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 (FT: 8.54 ± 0.9 nA; Δ2042–2368: 3.38 ± 0.89 nA (p<0.01); Δ2016–2368: 2.47 ± 0.89 nA (p<0.001); Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing statistically significant reductions in 3 ms EPSC amplitudes for these mutants (Figure 3, Table 2).

claim: Only the CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 mutants showed a significant slowdown in the 10–90 rise time compared to FT.
source: In addition, only the CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 mutants showed a significant slowdown in the 10–90 rise time compared to FT and a significant increases in the synaptic delay time (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing statistically significant increases in 10-90 rise time for these mutants (Table 2).

claim: Only the CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 mutants showed significant increases in the synaptic delay time.
source: In addition, only the CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 mutants showed a significant slowdown in the 10–90 rise time compared to FT and a significant increases in the synaptic delay time (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing statistically significant increases in synaptic delay for these mutants (Table 2).

claim: There was no significant change in the 10–90 rise time or EPSC amplitudes with CaV2.1Δ2365–2368, CaV2.1Δ2213–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2061–2368 in response to 30 ms step pulse compared to control.
source: In response to the 30 ms step pulse, we found no significant change in the 10–90 rise time or EPSC amplitudes with CaV2.1Δ2365–2368, CaV2.1Δ2213–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2061–2368 compared to control (Figure 2, Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no statistically significant differences for these parameters in these mutants (Table 2).

claim: The 30 ms 10–90 peak EPSC rise time is an inaccurate measure of coupling of all SVs in the total releasable pool.
source: It is important to note that unlike the 3 ms peak EPSC amplitude, the 30 ms 10–90 peak EPSC rise time is an inaccurate measure of coupling of all SVs in the total releasable pool, as the 30 ms peak amplitude does not accurately measure the total releasable pool size (Chen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Lee et al., 2012.

claim: There was a significant increase in the 10–90 rise time with CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 in response to 30 ms step pulse.
source: We found a significant increase in the 10–90 rise time with CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 (FT: 1.41 ± 0.18 ms; Δ2042–2368: 4.67 ± 0.72 ms (p<0.01); Δ2016–2368: 6.99 ± 1.45 ms (p<0.0001)), with reduced EPSC amplitudes (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing statistically significant increases in 10-90 rise time for 30 ms stimulation (Figure 3, Table 2).

claim: There was no difference between CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 in EPSC amplitude or 10–90 rise time.
source: In all cases, there was no difference between CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 indicating that the further deletion did not lead to more severe reductions in the ESPC amplitude or 10–90 rise time.
evidence: This is an observation from the data comparing these two mutants.

claim: A novel C-terminal region including at least the amino acids 2042–2061 is critical for fast release.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that a novel C-terminal region including at least the amino acids 2042–2061 is critical for fast release.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing dramatic effects on fast release with Δ2042–2368 and Δ2016–2368 but not with Δ2061–2368.

claim: Both CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 lead to a dramatic reduction in peak vesicle release rates.
source: We found that both CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 lead to a dramatic reduction in peak vesicle release rates (Figure 4) with a significant increase in the delayed release (slow pool component) and slower time to peak EPSC release rates compared to control (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by deconvolution analysis data showing reduced peak release rates (Figure 4A-B).

claim: Both CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 lead to a significant increase in the delayed release (slow pool component).
source: We found that both CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 lead to a dramatic reduction in peak vesicle release rates (Figure 4) with a significant increase in the delayed release (slow pool component) and slower time to peak EPSC release rates compared to control (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by deconvolution analysis data showing increased slow release component (Figure 4).

claim: Both CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 lead to slower time to peak EPSC release rates compared to control.
source: We found that both CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 lead to a dramatic reduction in peak vesicle release rates (Figure 4) with a significant increase in the delayed release (slow pool component) and slower time to peak EPSC release rates compared to control (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by deconvolution analysis data showing delayed time to peak (Figure 4).

claim: Both CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 lead to a dramatic reduction in both the fast pool and the total releasable pool.
source: Integration of the release rates for both the 3 ms and 30 ms pulses revealed a dramatic reduction in both mutants of both the fast pool and the total releasable pool. (RRP: FT: 1505 ± 245 SVs;Δ2042–2368: 430 ± 116 SVs (p<0.001); Δ2016–2368: 357 ± 134 SVs (p<0.001); total releasable pool: FT: 2152 ± 263 SVs; Δ2042–2368: 1292 ± 221 SVs (p<0.05); Δ2016–2368: 1061 ± 258 SVs (p<0.01)) (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by deconvolution analysis data showing statistically significant reductions in both RRP and total releasable pool sizes (Figure 4E-F).

claim: Both mutants (CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368) had a significantly decreased fast component of release.
source: This clearly demonstrates that both mutants had a significantly decreased fast component.
evidence: This claim is supported by normalized cumulative release data (Figure 4D).

claim: There was a significant reduction in the contribution of the RRP to the total releasable pool size in the CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 mutants.
source: Comparison of the ratio of the RPP size to the total releasable pool size revealed a significant reduction in the contribution of the RRP to the total releasable pool size in the mutants. (Figure 4G)(Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing statistically significant reductions in the 3ms/30ms EPSC ratio (Figure 4G, Table 3).

claim: The region between 2016 and 2042 is essential for regulating the total number of releasable vesicles.
source: Thus, based on our results we can conclude that the region between 2016 and 2042 is essential for both regulating the total number of releasable vesicles, as well as the relative contributions of fast and slow SV pool components.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing reductions in both RRP and total releasable pool with deletions in this region.

claim: The region between 2016 and 2042 is essential for regulating the relative contributions of fast and slow SV pool components.
source: Thus, based on our results we can conclude that the region between 2016 and 2042 is essential for both regulating the total number of releasable vesicles, as well as the relative contributions of fast and slow SV pool components.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing changes in the ratio of fast to total release with deletions in this region.

claim: Docked synaptic vesicles at the AZ are the morphological correlates of the RRP.
source: Since docked synaptic vesicles at the AZ are the morphological correlates of the RRP (Schikorski and Stevens, 2001), we next assessed how CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 affected presynaptic ultrastructure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schikorski and Stevens, 2001.

claim: AZ lengths were unchanged in CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 expressing calyces.
source: Analysis of EM images revealed that AZ lengths were unchanged (CaV2.1Δ2042–2368: 267.1 ± 8.1 nm vs. in slice control: 280.6 ± 8.2 nm (n = 120); CaV2.1Δ2016–2368:268. ± 7.9 nm vs. in slice control: 292.5 ± 8.1 nm (n = 100)), but revealed a specific reduction in only those SVs within 5 nm of the plasma membrane, in both CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 (CaV2.1Δ2042–2368: 0.77 ± 0.08 nmvs. in-slice control: 1.39 ± 0.1 (n = 120; p<0.0001); CaV2.1Δ2016–2368: 0.63 ± 0.08 nm vs. in-slice control:1.58 ± 0.12 nm (n = 100; p<0.0001) (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing no statistically significant differences in AZ length (Figure 5D, F).

claim: There was a specific reduction in only those SVs within 5 nm of the plasma membrane in both CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368.
source: Analysis of EM images revealed that AZ lengths were unchanged (CaV2.1Δ2042–2368: 267.1 ± 8.1 nm vs. in slice control: 280.6 ± 8.2 nm (n = 120); CaV2.1Δ2016–2368:268. ± 7.9 nm vs. in slice control: 292.5 ± 8.1 nm (n = 100)), but revealed a specific reduction in only those SVs within 5 nm of the plasma membrane, in both CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368 (CaV2.1Δ2042–2368: 0.77 ± 0.08 nmvs. in-slice control: 1.39 ± 0.1 (n = 120; p<0.0001); CaV2.1Δ2016–2368: 0.63 ± 0.08 nm vs. in-slice control:1.58 ± 0.12 nm (n = 100; p<0.0001) (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing statistically significant reductions in docked vesicles (Figure 5E, G).

claim: A motif or motifs in amino acids 2042–2061 in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit regulates RRP size and coupling.
source: Thus, our data demonstrates a motif or motif(s) in amino acids 2042–2061 in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit regulates RRP size and coupling (Figure 6).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined data showing effects on RRP size and release kinetics with deletions in this region without affecting Ca2+ currents.

claim: Loss of RIM resulted in a 2–3 fold slowdown in release kinetics at the prehearing calyx.
source: Prior studies using step depolarizations at the prehearing calyx have shown that loss of RIM and RBPs resulted in a 2–3 fold slowdown in release kinetics respectively and indicating that these proteins are involved in pathways that regulate the RRP size, coupling (Acuna et al., 2015; Han et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Acuna et al., 2015 and Han et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of RBPs resulted in a 2–3 fold slowdown in release kinetics at the prehearing calyx.
source: Prior studies using step depolarizations at the prehearing calyx have shown that loss of RIM and RBPs resulted in a 2–3 fold slowdown in release kinetics respectively and indicating that these proteins are involved in pathways that regulate the RRP size, coupling (Acuna et al., 2015; Han et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Acuna et al., 2015 and Han et al., 2011.

claim: Deletion of direct binding motifs for RIM or RBP in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit did not result in dramatic slowdown in release or changes in RRP size that mimicked the phenotypes seen with RIM or RBP KO animals.
source: In contrast, we did not see any dramatic slowdown in release or changes in RRP size that mimicked these phenotypes previously seen with RIM or RBP KO animals when these direct binding motifs in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit were deleted.
evidence: This is based on the data showing no significant effects with Δ2365–2368, Δ2213–2368, and Δ2061–2368 mutants.

claim: A CaV2.1 splice variant lacking RIM or RBP binding sites rescued AP-evoked release.
source: Although we observed a slight slowing of the 10–90 rise times, ~20–30%, which was similar for the Δ2365–2368, Δ2213–2368, Δ2061–2368 mutants, this was not statistically significant. We did not directly measure AP-evoked release in this study, but it has been previously demonstrated that a CaV2.1 splice variants lacking RIM or RBP binding sites rescued AP-evoked release (Cao and Tsien, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cao and Tsien, 2010.

claim: CaVβ interactions with RIM1/2 are critical for anchoring SVs to CaV2 calcium channels to control coupling in PC12 cells.
source: Finally, it has been demonstrated in PC12 cells that CaVβ interactions with RIM1/2 are critical for anchoring SVs to CaV2 calcium channels to control coupling (Uriu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Uriu et al., 2010.

claim: Proposed individual direct interactions between the CaV2.1 α1 subunit with RIM1/2 or RBP proteins at most play a minor role in regulating RRP size and coupling.
source: Thus, our results strongly support that proposed individual direct interactions in between the CaV2.1 α1 subunit with RIM1/2 (Han et al., 2011; Kaeser et al., 2011) or RBP proteins (Acuna et al., 2015; Hibino et al., 2002) at most play a minor role in regulating RRP size and coupling.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing no significant effects when these binding sites were deleted.

claim: There was a reduction in the total releasable pool size in addition to the reduction in RRP size with CaV2.1Δ2042–2368 and CaV2.1Δ2016–2368.
source: In addition to the reduction in RRP size, we observed a reduction in the total releasable pool size, indicating a loss in the number of fusion competent vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by the deconvolution analysis data (Figure 4F).

claim: The reduction in total releasable pool size corresponded to a 50% reduction in the number of docked SVs compared to wild-type.
source: Our morphological analysis revealed that this corresponded to a 50% reduction in the number of docked SVs compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data (Figure 5E, G).

claim: SV docking corresponds to priming.
source: Recent work proposed that SV docking corresponds to priming (Imig et al., 2014), therefore we propose that this region in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit is involved in priming.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Imig et al., 2014.

claim: The region 2042-2061 in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit is involved in priming.
source: Recent work proposed that SV docking corresponds to priming (Imig et al., 2014), therefore we propose that this region in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit is involved in priming.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed reduction in docked vesicles and the cited work linking docking to priming.

claim: The amino acid sequence of region 2042-2061 shows little homology to CaV2.2 and CaV2.3 α1 subunits.
source: Close inspection of the amino acid sequence reveals little homology to CaV2.2 and CaV2.3 α1 subunits (ClustalW-Gonnet series algorithm), however BLAST homology search reveals no known binding motifs (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis performed by the authors.

claim: BLAST homology search of region 2042-2061 reveals no known binding motifs.
source: Close inspection of the amino acid sequence reveals little homology to CaV2.2 and CaV2.3 α1 subunits (ClustalW-Gonnet series algorithm), however BLAST homology search reveals no known binding motifs (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis performed by the authors.

claim: Some presynaptic terminals transition from microdomain to nanodomain during maturation of neuronal circuits that encode temporal fidelity at high firing rates.
source: Despite containing CaV2.1, some presynaptic terminals transition from microdomain to nanodomain during maturation of neuronal circuits that encode temporal fidelity at high firing rates (Baur et al., 2015; Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baur et al., 2015 and Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005.

claim: Release states (nanodomain vs microdomain) are not specific to individual CaV2 subtypes.
source: Therefore, these release states are not specific to individual CaV2 subtypes, but instead the intrinsic motifs within the CaV2.1 α1 subunit are differentially utilized based on the developmental state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CaV2.1-containing terminals can exhibit different release modes.

claim: The intrinsic motifs within the CaV2.1 α1 subunit are differentially utilized based on the developmental state.
source: Therefore, these release states are not specific to individual CaV2 subtypes, but instead the intrinsic motifs within the CaV2.1 α1 subunit are differentially utilized based on the developmental state.
evidence: This is speculation based on the developmental changes in release mode.

claim: The study focused on the regulation of fast release at the prehearing calyx P9-11 which utilizes microdomain release mode.
source: Our results presented here focused solely on the regulation of fast release at the prehearing calyx P9-11 which utilizes microdomain release mode (Borst and Sakmann, 1996; Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions with citations to Borst and Sakmann, 1996 and Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005.

claim: The calyx transitions from microdomain to nanodomain release after the onset of hearing.
source: Since the calyx transitions from microdomain to nanodomain release after the onset of hearing it is highly possible that intrinsic motifs in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit dispensable for microdomain release are necessary to support nanodomain release.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the developmental changes in the calyx of Held.

claim: Intrinsic motifs in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit dispensable for microdomain release may be necessary to support nanodomain release.
source: Since the calyx transitions from microdomain to nanodomain release after the onset of hearing it is highly possible that intrinsic motifs in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit dispensable for microdomain release are necessary to support nanodomain release.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential role of different motifs at different developmental stages.

claim: Proteome composition at the AZ may vary in different presynaptic terminals.
source: Finally, since proteome composition at the AZ may vary in different various presynaptic terminals, different CaV2.1 motifs may or may not be essential to support coupling.
evidence: This is general knowledge about synaptic diversity.

claim: Different CaV2.1 motifs may or may not be essential to support coupling depending on the presynaptic terminal.
source: Finally, since proteome composition at the AZ may vary in different various presynaptic terminals, different CaV2.1 motifs may or may not be essential to support coupling.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential variability in motif requirements across different synapses.

claim: The findings counter the prevailing view that individual direct interactions between the CaV2.1 α1 subunit and RIM1/2, MINT, RBP proteins are crucial for controlling CaV2.1 abundance and coupling to SVs.
source: Taken together, these findings counter the prevailing views that (1) individual direct interactions between the CaV2.1 α1 subunit and RIM1/2, MINT, RBP proteins are crucial for controlling CaV2.1 abundance and coupling to SVs (Südhof, 2013) and (2) that PXXP motifs are involved in capturing and coupling SVs to calcium channels (Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing no significant effects when these binding sites were deleted, contrasting with the cited prevailing views.

claim: The findings counter the prevailing view that PXXP motifs are involved in capturing and coupling SVs to calcium channels.
source: Taken together, these findings counter the prevailing views that (1) individual direct interactions between the CaV2.1 α1 subunit and RIM1/2, MINT, RBP proteins are crucial for controlling CaV2.1 abundance and coupling to SVs (Südhof, 2013) and (2) that PXXP motifs are involved in capturing and coupling SVs to calcium channels (Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing no significant effects when PXXP motifs were deleted, contrasting with the cited prevailing view.

claim: The mechanisms of action by which known AZ proteins regulate SV coupling and CaV2.1 channel abundance involve indirect interactions with protein(s) that bind directly to the CaV2.1 α1 subunit.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the mechanisms of action by which known AZ proteins regulate SV coupling and CaV2.1 channel abundance involve indirect interactions with protein(s) that bind directly to the CaV2.1 α1 subunit.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings that direct binding sites are not necessary, suggesting indirect mechanisms.

claim: The Cacna1a conditional knock-out mouse line circumvents potential artifacts due to global loss of CaV2.1 in the brain and lethality issues in the Cacna1a KO mouse line.
source: In our study, we specifically ablated the CaV2.1 α1 subunit in the calyx of Held using a flox mouse line of the CaV2.1 α1 subunit (Todorov et al., 2006) which circumvents potential artifacts due to global loss of CaV2.1 in the brain and lethality issues in the Cacna1a KO mouse line (Jun et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a methodological advantage of the conditional knockout approach, supported by citations.

claim: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit cDNA is larger than 7 kb.
source: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit (>7 kb cDNA), (Catterall, 2011) is larger than common viral vectors such as recombinant Adeno-associated virus (rAAV) or lentiviral vectors (rLVV), 5 kb and 9 kb maximum packaging capacity (Lentz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the size of the CaV2.1 α1 subunit cDNA, supported by citation to Catterall, 2011.

claim: Recombinant Adeno-associated virus has a maximum packaging capacity of 5 kb.
source: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit (>7 kb cDNA), (Catterall, 2011) is larger than common viral vectors such as recombinant Adeno-associated virus (rAAV) or lentiviral vectors (rLVV), 5 kb and 9 kb maximum packaging capacity (Lentz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a factual statement about rAAV packaging capacity, supported by citation to Lentz et al., 2012.

claim: Lentiviral vectors have a maximum packaging capacity of 9 kb.
source: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit (>7 kb cDNA), (Catterall, 2011) is larger than common viral vectors such as recombinant Adeno-associated virus (rAAV) or lentiviral vectors (rLVV), 5 kb and 9 kb maximum packaging capacity (Lentz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a factual statement about lentiviral vector packaging capacity, supported by citation to Lentz et al., 2012.

claim: HdAd vectors permit packaging of up to 37 kb of foreign DNA.
source: To overcome these challenges we utilized HdAd vectors which supplant earlier versions of recombinant Ad technology, permit packaging of up to 37 kb of foreign DNA, overcome the limitations of rAAV and rLVV, and do not impact neuronal viability (Montesinos et al., 2016; Muhammad et al., 2012; Palmer and Ng, 2003; Palmer and Ng, 2005).
evidence: This is a factual statement about HdAd vector capacity, supported by multiple citations.

claim: HdAd vectors do not impact neuronal viability.
source: To overcome these challenges we utilized HdAd vectors which supplant earlier versions of recombinant Ad technology, permit packaging of up to 37 kb of foreign DNA, overcome the limitations of rAAV and rLVV, and do not impact neuronal viability (Montesinos et al., 2016; Muhammad et al., 2012; Palmer and Ng, 2003; Palmer and Ng, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Montesinos et al., 2016; Muhammad et al., 2012; Palmer and Ng, 2003; Palmer and Ng, 2005.

claim: The human synapsin promoter used is a relatively weak promoter and does not lead to massive overexpression as seen with CMV or CBA promoters.
source: This promoter is a relatively weak promoter and does not lead to massive overexpression as seen with CMV or CBA promoters (Glover et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Glover et al., 2002.

claim: CaV2.1 α1 subunit expression with HdAd vectors in the CaV2.1−/− background led to similar Ca2+ current amplitudes as wild-type.
source: Our rescue experiments showed CaV2.1 α1 subunit expression with our HdAd vectors in the CaV2.1−/− background lead to similar Ca2+ current amplitudes, CaV2.1 subtype levels and similar SV release rates as wild-type, thereby validating our experimental approach (Figure 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing wild-type and full transcript rescue (Figure 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: CaV2.1 α1 subunit expression with HdAd vectors in the CaV2.1−/− background led to similar CaV2.1 subtype levels as wild-type.
source: Our rescue experiments showed CaV2.1 α1 subunit expression with our HdAd vectors in the CaV2.1−/− background lead to similar Ca2+ current amplitudes, CaV2.1 subtype levels and similar SV release rates as wild-type, thereby validating our experimental approach (Figure 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological data showing similar CaV2.1 fractions (Figure 1F).

claim: CaV2.1 α1 subunit expression with HdAd vectors in the CaV2.1−/− background led to similar SV release rates as wild-type.
source: Our rescue experiments showed CaV2.1 α1 subunit expression with our HdAd vectors in the CaV2.1−/− background lead to similar Ca2+ current amplitudes, CaV2.1 subtype levels and similar SV release rates as wild-type, thereby validating our experimental approach (Figure 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing wild-type and full transcript rescue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit splice variant lacking the RIM1/2, RBP, or MINT1 binding sites is localized to the presynaptic terminal.
source: Our results are similar to those studies (Cao and Tsien, 2010; Hu et al., 2005) that expressed the CaV2.1 α1 subunit splice variant lacking the RIM1/2, RBP, or MINT1 binding sites (Soong et al., 2002). This splice variant is localized to the presynaptic terminal (Hu et al., 2005) and could rescue the CaV2.1 channel contribution to AP evoked release in Cacna1a KO primary hippocampal neurons (Cao and Tsien, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2005.

claim: The CaV2.1 α1 subunit splice variant lacking the RIM1/2, RBP, or MINT1 binding sites could rescue the CaV2.1 channel contribution to AP evoked release in Cacna1a KO primary hippocampal neurons.
source: Our results are similar to those studies (Cao and Tsien, 2010; Hu et al., 2005) that expressed the CaV2.1 α1 subunit splice variant lacking the RIM1/2, RBP, or MINT1 binding sites (Soong et al., 2002). This splice variant is localized to the presynaptic terminal (Hu et al., 2005) and could rescue the CaV2.1 channel contribution to AP evoked release in Cacna1a KO primary hippocampal neurons (Cao and Tsien, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cao and Tsien, 2010.

claim: Cask KO had no impact on basal AP-evoked release kinetics.
source: Furthermore, our data is in line with studies from Cask KO (Atasoy et al., 2007) and X11α KO (Ho et al., 2003) which had no impact on basal AP-evoked release kinetics and Rim-bp1/ Rim-bp2 cKO (Acuna et al., 2015) animals which demonstrated no loss of CaV2.1 current density.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Atasoy et al., 2007.

claim: X11α KO had no impact on basal AP-evoked release kinetics.
source: Furthermore, our data is in line with studies from Cask KO (Atasoy et al., 2007) and X11α KO (Ho et al., 2003) which had no impact on basal AP-evoked release kinetics and Rim-bp1/ Rim-bp2 cKO (Acuna et al., 2015) animals which demonstrated no loss of CaV2.1 current density.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ho et al., 2003.

claim: Rim-bp1/Rim-bp2 cKO animals demonstrated no loss of CaV2.1 current density.
source: Furthermore, our data is in line with studies from Cask KO (Atasoy et al., 2007) and X11α KO (Ho et al., 2003) which had no impact on basal AP-evoked release kinetics and Rim-bp1/ Rim-bp2 cKO (Acuna et al., 2015) animals which demonstrated no loss of CaV2.1 current density.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Acuna et al., 2015.

claim: The results do not support the model in which Bassoon regulates CaV2.1 abundance at the presynaptic terminal through direct RBP interaction with the CaV2.1 α1 subunit.
source: Although our results cannot rule out that Bassoon controls CaV2.1 abundance, our results do not support the model in which Bassoon regulates CaV2.1 abundance at the presynaptic terminal through direct RBP interaction with the CaV2.1 α1 subunit (Davydova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that deletion of RBP binding sites does not affect CaV2.1 abundance.

claim: RIM proteins are important for regulating CaV2 channel current density and abundance at both invertebrate and vertebrate presynaptic terminals.
source: RIM proteins have been demonstrated to be important for regulating CaV2 channel current density and abundance at both invertebrate and vertebrate presynaptic terminals, as knock out RIM proteins lead to dramatic reductions in Ca2+ currents (Graf et al., 2012; Han et al., 2011; Kaeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Graf et al., 2012; Han et al., 2011; Kaeser et al., 2011.

claim: Knock out of RIM proteins leads to dramatic reductions in Ca2+ currents.
source: RIM proteins have been demonstrated to be important for regulating CaV2 channel current density and abundance at both invertebrate and vertebrate presynaptic terminals, as knock out RIM proteins lead to dramatic reductions in Ca2+ currents (Graf et al., 2012; Han et al., 2011; Kaeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Graf et al., 2012; Han et al., 2011; Kaeser et al., 2011.

claim: Deletion of the DDWC motif in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit did not lead to any changes in CaV2.1 currents.
source: However, deletion of the DDWC motif in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit which interacts both with MINT1 and RIM1/2 did not lead to any changes in CaV2.1 currents (Figures 2 and 3) indicating this motif is not necessary for CaV2.1 targeting to the presynaptic membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in Ca2+ currents with the Δ2365–2368 mutant (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: The DDWC motif is not necessary for CaV2.1 targeting to the presynaptic membrane.
source: However, deletion of the DDWC motif in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit which interacts both with MINT1 and RIM1/2 did not lead to any changes in CaV2.1 currents (Figures 2 and 3) indicating this motif is not necessary for CaV2.1 targeting to the presynaptic membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing no changes in Ca2+ currents when the DDWC motif was deleted.

claim: The necessity of the RIM PDZ domain interaction with the CaV2.1 α1 subunit DDWC was not directly demonstrated in vivo.
source: Although the RIM1/2 PDZ domain interaction with the CaV2.1 α1 subunit DDWC is proposed to be critical for CaV2.1/2.2 abundance and localization to the presynaptic terminal, the necessity of this interaction was not directly demonstrated in vivo (Kaeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior literature, noting a limitation in the cited study.

claim: Other biochemical assays have failed to detect the direct interaction between RIM PDZ domain and CaV2.1 α1 subunit.
source: Furthermore, other biochemical assays have failed to detect this direct interaction (Wong et al., 2013, 2014; Wong and Stanley, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wong et al., 2013, 2014; Wong and Stanley, 2010.

claim: The RIM PDZ domain interacts with CAST/ELKS proteins with an affinity of 200 nM.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that the RIM PDZ domain interacts with the CAST/ELKS proteins with an affinity of 200 nM (Lu et al., 2005), while the RIM PDZ domain interaction with the CaV2.1/2.2 α1 subunit has an affinity of 20 µM (Kaeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2005.

claim: The RIM PDZ domain interaction with the CaV2.1/2.2 α1 subunit has an affinity of 20 µM.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that the RIM PDZ domain interacts with the CAST/ELKS proteins with an affinity of 200 nM (Lu et al., 2005), while the RIM PDZ domain interaction with the CaV2.1/2.2 α1 subunit has an affinity of 20 µM (Kaeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaeser et al., 2011.

claim: RIM1/2 PDZ may interact with CAST/ELKS proteins to form a macromolecular complex that controls CaV2.1/2.2 abundance.
source: Thus, an alternative interpretation is that RIM1/2 PDZ interacts with CAST/ELKS proteins to form a macromolecular complex that controls CaV2.1/2.2 abundance (Hida and Ohtsuka, 2010).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism, supported by citation to Hida and Ohtsuka, 2010.

claim: The synprint region which binds to SNARE proteins has been proposed to be an integral motif for CaV2.1 incorporation into the presynaptic terminal.
source: What then could be the motifs that are essential for CaV2.1 localization/abundance at the presynaptic terminal? In addition to the C-terminal region, the synprint region which binds to SNARE proteins has been proposed to be an integral motif for CaV2.1 incorporation into the presynaptic terminal (Catterall, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Catterall, 2011.

claim: Syntaxin 1A binding sites in CaV2.2 are dispensable for synaptic targeting and AP-evoked release.
source: However, syntaxin 1A binding sites in CaV2.2 are dispensable for synaptic targeting and AP-evoked release (Szabo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szabo et al., 2006.

claim: Synprint domains lacking syntaxin 1A binding sites have reduced levels of incorporation into the neuroendocrine cell membranes.
source: Interestingly, synprint domains lacking syntaxin 1A binding sites have reduced levels of incorporation into the neuroendocrine cell membranes (Rajapaksha et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rajapaksha et al., 2008.

claim: The AID domain in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit interacts with the CaVβ subunit to regulate CaV2.1 localization to the presynaptic membrane via a RIM1/2-dependent mechanism.
source: Another potential motif is the AID domain in the CaV2.1 α1 subunit which interacts with the CaVβ subunit to regulate CaV2.1 localization to the presynaptic membrane via a RIM1/2-dependent mechanism (Kiyonaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kiyonaka et al., 2007.

claim: No single motif may be responsible for CaV2.1 localization and incorporation in the presynaptic membrane, but various motifs may act in concert or independently.
source: Since the CaV2.1 α1 subunit is heavily spliced depending on the neuronal cell-type (Simms and Zamponi, 2014), it is possible that no single motif is responsible for CaV2.1 localization and incorporation in the presynaptic membrane, but that various motifs may act in concert or independently to ensure CaV2.1 abundance.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential redundancy or combinatorial nature of motifs regulating CaV2.1 localization.

claim: The necessity of motifs for CaV2.1 localization may vary at different synapses and the developmental state of the neuronal circuit.
source: In addition, the necessity of these motifs may also vary at different synapses and the developmental state of the neuronal circuit in which the synapses are embedded.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential context-dependence of motif requirements.

claim: CaV2.1 channels are not randomly distributed in the presynaptic membrane but cluster within AZs.
source: CaV2.1 channels are not randomly distributed in the presynaptic membrane but cluster within AZs (Holderith et al., 2012; Nakamura et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Holderith et al., 2012 and Nakamura et al., 2015.

claim: The conclusions based on presynaptic recordings are limited to CaV2.1 localization to the presynaptic terminal, not clustering within individual AZs.
source: Since the calyx of Held is a large presynaptic terminal that contains many AZs, the conclusions based our presynaptic recordings are limited to CaV2.1 localization to the presynaptic terminal. Thus, we cannot rule out that the C-terminal domains contained within amino acids 2016–2368 which are not essential for localization to the presynaptic membrane, are critical for CaV2.1 clustering/organization within individual AZs.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: Exons 44–47 of CaV2.1 can impact voltage dependent activation and inactivation in HEK293 cells.
source: Although exons 44–47 of CaV2.1 can impact voltage dependent activation and inactivation in HEK293 cells (Hirano et al., 2017), our direct recordings did not detect differences in the overall biophysical parameters of these mutants compared to terminals rescued with full length CaV2.1 α1 subunits or in a wild-type background.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hirano et al., 2017.

claim: Direct recordings did not detect differences in the overall biophysical parameters of the mutants compared to terminals rescued with full length CaV2.1 α1 subunits or in a wild-type background.
source: Although exons 44–47 of CaV2.1 can impact voltage dependent activation and inactivation in HEK293 cells (Hirano et al., 2017), our direct recordings did not detect differences in the overall biophysical parameters of these mutants compared to terminals rescued with full length CaV2.1 α1 subunits or in a wild-type background.
